item.title: How Does AI Make Us Stupid?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How Does AI Make Us Stupid?

Lessons from 2003 are still relevant as we weigh the risks of today's AI.

Posted November 14, 2026

Key points
  • Generative AI is achieving incredible outcomes but possibly at the cost of a deterioration of our expertise.
  • I cataloged some of these degradations in 2003 with regard to the use of information technology.
  • Current AI may make us worse at recognizing patterns, searching for data, and improving our mental models.
  • The challenge is to understand the basis of expertise in order to safeguard and enhance it.

Current versions of artificial intelligence have created so much well-deserved excitement. However, along with all that progress has come a wave of apprehension about the destructive potential of using AI. Fears that AI could be harming us. Fears that it might be making us stupid.

I wrote about this possibility in 2019, in a post I titled "The Second Singularity," and I am not happy to see my predictions coming true.

However, this post asks a different question. Now I am looking back to 2003 and the original publication of my book The Power of Intuition. This was before large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Claude and the generative AI technologies. My book examined different facets of intuition/expertise. Chapter 16 was titled “Smart Technology Can Make Us Stupid.” The smart technology I was writing about was simply the 2003-style information technology, not current LLMs, but the mechanisms I identified seem quite relevant today.

In that chapter, I wrote, “Information technologies are intended to make us more productive, but their use carries a penalty. The computer programs, the decision support systems, the search engines, databases, and shareware we use can diminish our intuition and expertise. They can make us stupid.” I worried that the 2003-era technologies could disable our expertise, or at least slow down our acquisition of expertise, or, more ominously, teach dysfunctional skills that interfered with expertise.

But how would that work? In 2003, I identified several possibilities.

Recognizing patterns. That’s something we are good at—spotting patterns in data, seeing trends, seeing anomalies, spotting nonevents. But information technology “helps” us by doing the analyses for us, since the high data flows make it impossible for us to examine all or even most of the data. So we are removed from direct access to the data and removed from our ability to spot patterns.

For example, in one project we conducted on weather forecasters, a technologist at a weather forecasting conference explained how his system helpfully smoothed the data in order to highlight trends. Most of the audience appreciated this assistance, but the experienced forecasters in the room winced—they wanted to see the noise because that was where turbulence was going to affect the weather picture. The smoothing was removing a critical cue.

Searching for data. That’s another important human ability—to adaptively search through data. However, information technologies often organize the search space in advance and define the basic level of detail. But in complex settings there is no basic level of detail, and the appropriate level of detail depends on what you are searching for and what you are finding. The relevant data depend on how you are interpreting the situation, a phenomenon called the relevance realization process (Vervaeke et al., 2012)—skimming through the large amounts of data to identify what matters. Information technologies can reduce their users to passive recipients of data rather than active sensemakers.

Mental models. As we gain expertise, we are acquiring richer mental models about the phenomena we are interacting with. But information technology can weaken our mental models by keeping us tethered to the original categories we started our searches and analyses with. Decision-makers may have to set up categories in advance, and subsequent events may tie them into these categories rather than allowing and supporting the evolution of categories based on new experiences.

The story behind the data. As we gain expertise, we learn more about how the data were collected, and we become sensitive to limitations in the data collection process. However, information technology often makes it difficult to trace the story of the data and to appreciate how the data were collected and synthesized—the pedigree of the data. Borders et al. (2024) presented a mental model matrix that highlighted the importance of understanding the limitations and boundary conditions of a system in order to work effectively with it. However, if we don’t know the pedigree of the data, we will struggle to identify boundary conditions.

Adaptability. This is a critical function of expertise—being able to pivot based on discoveries about what is really going on in a situation. Unfortunately, many information technologies can go off the rails if we don’t follow the prescribed procedures for interacting with them or if we don’t follow the steps that have been laid out. As a result, it can become more difficult for us to improvise when new and unexpected conditions arise. When we stray from the prescribed path, we are likely to be bombarded with error messages, discouraging us from adapting.

Active stance. With expertise comes an active stance of taking charge and making things happen. Yet information technologies can shift us into a passive stance, unthinkingly accepting the recommendations of the system. Here the link to LLMs is particularly strong, as users relying on LLMs contentedly accept their products, often without doing any kind of due diligence.

Conclusion

These are the attributes of expertise that information technologies seemed to jeopardize, in my 2003 analysis. Fast-forward two decades. Most of these attributes also seem threatened today by the spread of generative AI. I leave it to readers to gauge how closely the generative AI dysfunctions map onto the earlier information technology problems. At the very least, I hope this post will be helpful in unpacking what may be contributing to today’s generative AI dysfunctions. The challenge is to better understand the basis of expertise in order to find ways to safeguard and enhance it.

item.title: How to Increase Psychological Safety Amid Chronic Illness
item.description:
Chronic Illness

How to Increase Psychological Safety Amid Chronic Illness

Befriend the body to help build a sense of psychological safety.

Posted November 14, 2026

Key points
  • Psychological safety is "read" through body sensations.
  • Living with chronic illness can impede a positive relationship with the body.
  • Consciously working to deepen one's relationship with the body can improve psychological safety.
Source: Katie Willard-Virant

How safe do you feel in this moment? Pause what you are doing, close your eyes, take a couple of deep breaths, and tune in to your body. Start at your feet and work up, scanning your body with your mind’s eye. Are there places where your muscles feel tense? Is your breathing shallow? Is it hard to tune in to your body because your mind will not settle? Don’t try to change anything right now. Just notice the sensations you are having in this moment.

Psychological safety is defined as “a person’s capacity to experience the self, the body, and the interpersonal environment as sufficiently safe to sustain openness, affect regulation, and adaptive engagement" (Poli & Miccoli, 2026). The body “is one of the main channels through which safety, threat, and dysregulation are experienced" (Poli & Miccoli, 2026).

Safety is a continuum. We feel safe (and unsafe) by degrees. Typically, we have conscious awareness of when we are at either end of this continuum. We know when we feel safe, for example, when our muscles are relaxed, and our thoughts are pleasant. At those moments, we enjoy the positive sensations in our body that let us know, “I am happy. I am safe.” Conversely, we know when we feel very unsafe. Our heart rate goes up; we may feel nauseated or light-headed; breathing may feel labored. We interpret these sensations as a lack of safety.

The middle of the safety continuum is where we spend the vast majority of our time. Without the extremes of body sensations that occur at either end of the continuum, we often tune out the body, putting it outside of our consciousness. Paying attention to body sensations in the middle of the safety continuum can lead to a deeper relationship with the body and greater psychological safety.

Chronic Illness and Psychological Safety

Many people living with illness describe their relationship with their body as challenging. Lack of trust in the body, anger at the body, and alienation from the body are all sequelae of chronic illness (Taylor, Morton, & Cogan, 2026). Questions like “How safe do you feel in this moment?” are complicated by the bodily mistrust that chronic illness perpetuates. Illness “disrupts...the felt sense of psychological safety" (Taylor, Morton, & Cogan, 2026).

Growing Psychological Safety in Chronic Illness

In order to grow psychological safety, we must have an intentional relationship with our body. Take a few moments and ascertain what that relationship currently looks like. Write a few sentences responding to each of the following statements. How true or false does each statement feel to you?

  • I am wary of my body.
  • I wish I didn’t have a body.
  • I hate my body.
  • My body is the site of pleasure as well as pain.
  • I can rely on my body sometimes.
  • I like my body.
  • I love my body.

Now that you have a sense of your current relationship with your body, write a few sentences about how you would like this relationship to be different. Some ideas might be: “I’d like to feel less hostile toward my body” or “I’d like to appreciate my body for the things it can do, rather than be solely focused on the ways it disappoints me.”

If you were seeking to improve a relationship with another person, you’d likely (a) spend intentional time with them, and (b) have open communication with them. Similarly, in improving your relationship with your body, you will want to carve out intentional time together and increase honest communication (both listening and feeling heard).

In order to relate harmoniously with our body, we have to get to know it. In order to know it, we have to spend intentional time with it. What you do during this time is less important than your non-distracted presence. You could take a shower or bath, go for a walk, do a yoga session, or simply sit quietly and follow your breath. You want to be present during your time with your body. Notice without trying to change the sensations that come up.

You’re also going to want to communicate with your body during these “being with” sessions. You can speak aloud or in your mind, or journal. Just put words to the sensations you have, being as honest as possible. You might say, “This is really stupid. I feel fidgety and anxious. It’s frustrating to be with you, body.” Perhaps you have a different experience and say, “I feel vulnerable and shy. I’m not used to showing up in my body like this.” It may be that you feel a lessening of tension, such that you say, “Wow, this feels nice to be with my body, undistracted by other concerns.”

Open your mind, too, to the ways your body is communicating with you during these sessions. Be curious. Maybe your body is whispering, “I’m tired. I do the best I can, and I don’t feel very appreciated.” Perhaps your body is screaming, “I hurt! I’m angry and agitated, and I need some relief!” It’s possible that your body is saying, “I feel you tuning in to me, and I have been waiting a long time for your presence.”

Conclusion

Make it a habit to communicate with your body in the ways described above. Your body is constantly changing, and your experiences of tuning in to it will be variable. Stay open and curious; let yourself be surprised.

Psychological safety depends upon a connection between body and psyche. Working to deepen that connection is an important tool in managing chronic illness.

item.title: The Potential Benefits of Using an Anglo First Name
item.description:
Identity

The Potential Benefits of Using an Anglo First Name

Studies show job applicants fare better when they use an American-sounding name.

Posted November 14, 2026

Key points
  • Adopting an Anglo name increased perceived similarity to Americans in studies with White participants.
  • Students who value assimilation rated Anglo-named speakers more favorably than Chinese-named ones.
  • Adopting an Anglo name may lower self-esteem, despite potential social and career benefits.

Many Psychology Today readers are familiar with the dispiriting findings of studies conducted by social scientists: When they apply for jobs or housing, persons with ethnic minority names (like Lakeisha and Abdullah) are generally treated less well than persons with majority group names (like Daniel and Jennifer).

Will foreigners in the United States and Americans with foreign-sounding names be treated better if they adopt an Anglicized name? Would the immensely successful Nvidia executive Jensen Huang have been less successful in business if he had used his birth name, Jen-Hsun?

Two University of Kansas researchers, Xian Zhao and Monica Biernat, have conducted three studies that investigate the potential benefits that may accrue to foreigners who choose to use an Anglo name.

Different Names, Different Outcomes

In the first study, 102 Americans—almost all of them White—looked at four photos of Chinese students who were attending college in the United States. Some participants saw photos that were labeled with an Anglo name like Andrew. Others saw photos that showed a Chinese name like Xiang. The participants used a 7-point scale to rate the similarity of each target “to Americans.”

On average, the pictured individuals with Anglo names were rated as more similar to Americans, and the ones with Chinese names were rated as less similar. The difference wasn’t large—about a half-point on the 7-point scale—but it was statistically significant.

In the second study, more than 400 college professors around the U.S. received an e-mail from “a student from China” who asked to meet and talk about the possibility of assisting with the professor’s research. Some professors received an e-mail in which the student introduced himself as Xian Zhao. Others received an e-mail in which the student introduced himself as “Xian Zhao, but you can call me by my English name Alex.” In every other way, the e-mail requests were identical.

The different names affected the likelihood of getting a response. The “Alex” version received responses from 62 percent of the professors, while the “Xian” version received a response from just 53 percent.

In the third study, 184 undergraduates—almost all of them White—listened to a four-minute mini-lecture about affective forecasting. The lecturer introduced himself as a student from China who was pursuing a doctorate in social psychology at the university. In one version of the recording, the lecturer said, “Hi everyone. My name is Jian.” In another version, he said, “Hi everyone. My name is John” (an Anglicized version of Jian). In every other way, the recorded lectures were identical.

The participants were told to listen carefully to the lecture and then candidly evaluate the speaker because the department was “screening and selecting Ph.D. students to be instructors.” The participants also indicated the degree to which they support components of multiculturalism (wanting to learn from other cultural groups, for example) and the degree to which they believe that people who come to the United States should change their behavior to be more like Americans.

The participants evaluated the lecturer more favorably when he used an Anglo name and less favorably when he used his original Chinese name, but only among participants who rejected multiculturalism and believed foreigners should assimilate to local norms.

The opposite pattern was observed among participants who endorsed multiculturalism and did not endorse assimilationism. Those participants actually evaluated the lecturer more favorably when he used his original Chinese name.

A Double-Edged Sword?

The differences observed in these studies were not large, but the bottom line seems clear: Chinese students in the United States—and perhaps other international students—can potentially benefit by choosing to use an Anglo name, especially in more parochial parts of the country.

This strategy, however, may also have a downside. In an earlier post, I reported the results of a 2018 study conducted by the same two Kansas researchers. In that study, Chinese students in the U.S. who adopted an Anglicized name reported slightly lower levels of self-esteem.

It seems that adopting an Anglo name can be a double-edged sword for foreigners. Some employers may evaluate Jian Li slightly lower than John Lee, but Jian may feel somewhat better about himself than John does.

item.title: Harness Neuroscience to Improve Psychological First Aid
item.description:
Disaster Psychology

Harness Neuroscience to Improve Psychological First Aid

Brain mapping may help us be more effective helping others in distress.

Posted November 14, 2026

Key points
  • Psychological first aid (PFA) is becoming an essential tool in community mental health and disaster response.
  • Improving the efficiency and effectiveness of PFA may be an important quest.
  • Neuroscience may help us refine PFA to externally stimulate brain regions responsible for natural resilience.
Source: johnhain / Pixabay

Psychological first aid (PFA) may be the first and most effective of psychological crisis interventions. Recommended by the World Health Organization, the United Nations, the American Red Cross, and the American Psychological Association, it is not only being applied in disaster settings but is also being used to expand psychological support in communities in non-disaster situations. While research has demonstrated that PFA can be effective, training in how to apply PFA would seem essential. A recent study by Watanabe and others (Watanabe et al., 2026) on the neuroscience of the resilient brain may improve the efficiency of PFA by identifying the brain regions PFA should target.

The Resilient Brain

Menon's (2011) Triple Network Model proposes that three large-scale brain networks serve as the underlying neural circuits for attention and cognitive appraisal, emotion, and reactive adaptive behavior. Dysregulation of these networks is believed to be the neurological underpinning of low resilience and distress during and in the wake of crisis. Conversely, highly integrated and complementary functioning within these same areas appears to be the neurological underpinning of resilience and adaptive functioning.

The Triple Network consists of the salience network (SN), the default mode network (DMN), and the executive control network (ECN). The SN prioritizes incoming information, assesses importance, detects threats, directs attention, and mobilizes defense mechanisms. It answers the question “What happened and what’s really important in this moment?” The DMN is the neural foundation for self-reflection, retrospection, introspection, and making meaning out of experiences. It is also involved in social connection. The DMN answers the question, “What does this mean to me?” The ECN engages working memory for planning, problem-solving, and goal-directed behavior. This network allows individuals to exert top-down cognitive control over emotion and implement effective coping strategies. The ECN answers the question, “How should I react?” Based on the determination of the DMN, the ECN can then also answer the question, ”Is there another way of interpreting this?” The ECN and DMN collaborate for problem-solving, cognitive reappraisal, and fostering adaptive coping.

Research has found that resilient individuals show increased activity and interaction between the DMN and the ECN with diminished activity in the SN. Less resilient individuals show increased and prolonged activity in the SN.

Questions May Be the Neural Catalyst for Resilience

The work of Menon may provide a working heuristic as a foundation for practical application. So, perhaps the effectiveness of PFA can be enhanced by using interventions that target the resilience mechanisms residing in the DMN and the ECN while dampening the SN. More specifically, the neuroimaging literature on resilience suggests that PFA might be used to induce, externally, the same functional brain state that resilient individuals appear to achieve internally.

When assisting a person in crisis, numerous sources have proposed that asking questions may be more effective than providing immediate answers (Everly & Lating, 2026). A simple set of questions targeting Menon’s Triple Network may help improve the efficiency and perhaps the effectiveness of PFA:

  1. “What happened?” (SN)
  2. “How bad is it?” (SN)
  3. “Why is this important in this moment?” (SN)
  4. “What does this mean?” (DMN)
  5. “Does it really warrant this much attention and energy?” (DMN)
  6. “Is there another way of interpreting the situation?” (ECN)
  7. “What is the best response?” (ECN)

The research also suggests the window for promoting resilience may come after 60 minutes or more, as the SN takes physiological priority in the first hour.

While intuition would suggest solving the immediate problem is always the best crisis intervention, that may not be true in all cases. The notion of using questions to catalyze reflection and introspection (DMN) and foster reappraisal (ECN) is not new. Socrates, often considered the greatest teacher of his time, embraced the question rather than the answer as a means of teaching and empowering. Perhaps that is a lesson we all can learn as we endeavor to assist others in distress.

© 2026, George S. Everly, Jr., PhD.

item.title: Why I Left Finance to Start a Shrimp Charity
item.description:
Behavioral Finance

Why I Left Finance to Start a Shrimp Charity

An interview with Andrés Jiménez Zorrilla, founder of the Shrimp Welfare Project.

Posted November 14, 2026

Why would anyone leave a lucrative career in finance to create a charity for shrimps?

Yesterday, I interviewed (watch the full interview here) Andrés Jiménez Zorrilla, one of the two co-founders of the Shrimp Welfare Project, to find out. An edited transcript is below.

Walter Veit: Let us start with your background. Who are you, and how did you first become interested in shrimps?

Andrés Jiménez Zorrilla: I was born and raised in Mexico. I married my high school sweetheart; we have been together for more than 20 years and have two kids. I studied economics, then spent more than 15 years in finance: investment banking, private equity, and so on. I have launched five ventures, some for-profit and some not-for-profit, including Shrimp Welfare Project, and I have lived a nomadic life across three continents for half my adult life.

I launched Shrimp Welfare Project for two reasons. I cared about animals, and I had found effective altruism and bought into the idea that evidence, reason, and scope sensitivity matter enormously. Put those together, and you arrive at caring a great deal about shrimp welfare.

WV: Did you always have an interest in animals?

AJZ: Not really. I liked animals the way most people do. I grew up with a dog, and my family had a farm, but animals did not occupy much mental space, and certainly not my career. My wife was different. She is a very caring person by nature. When we lived in London, she worked helping women leaving prison reintegrate into society, and many of her colleagues were animal advocates in their spare time. She became one too and tried to convince me it was worthwhile.

It took me a long while to believe her. For the longest time I thought: that is nice for someone with spare time, but I work in finance. I have a serious job. I go to Canary Wharf every day. Little by little, though, the strength of her arguments chipped away at my doubts, and when I decided to leave finance, that was what I wanted to dedicate my time to.

WV: That is quite similar to my own path. Until recently, philosophers did not talk much about animals. There was Thomas Nagel’s famous paper, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” which argued that we can never really know what it is like to be another animal. Then Peter Godfrey-Smith came along. But for me it was really my wife. When we met, she was writing a Ph.D. thesis on how we can study animal welfare, and we began writing about it together. She also cured me of an early bias: I worried that a philosopher who got too close to activism would look less objective. That was a mistake.

article continues after advertisement

AJZ: Well, I am very grateful to your wife for that, because I am very grateful for your work and your writing.

WV: She worked as a zookeeper before becoming a philosopher, and she was involved with effective altruism, visiting the Global Priorities Institute, so she pulled me in that direction too. Now, in some of your interviews, it sounded as though you were initially unsure what kind of project to start. How did you end up choosing shrimps? Why shrimps?

AJZ: There are many layers to that. My wife’s day job was working with refugees, in children’s hospices, or helping women reintegrate into society, so she had a broad portfolio of ways of doing good. At some point I decided I wanted that too. By the time I left finance, around 2018, I cared a lot about animals, but also about many other cause areas, and I struggled to work out where I could actually have an impact.

Then a good friend of ours emailed my wife about a programme for launching charities, run by what is now Ambitious Impact and then called Charity Entrepreneurship. By her own admission, she found it too nerdy: all those numbers, all those spreadsheets. So she forwarded it to me and said that this looks up your alley.

It was a stark contrast to everything else I had been exploring. At one point we had considered buying land in Spain, where we lived at the time, and running an animal sanctuary. I thought that mattered, but I was grossly unprepared and almost scared of having animals in my care. I think I avoided a train wreck. The way effective altruism talks about doing good, following reason and evidence but ambitiously, at scale, really spoke to me. I applied, went very deep into effective altruism as fast as I could so I would not flop the interviews, and got in.

The programme identifies ideas that are important, neglected, and potentially tractable, and not only in animal welfare. My cohort was offered all kinds of super interesting options, including an organisation to optimise the taxation of alcohol, whose burden of disease is huge and, in my opinion, underappreciated. There were ideas in family planning and a couple in animal welfare. Fortunately and unfortunately, I was drawn to every one of them.

article continues after advertisement

In the end, I relied on a heuristic effective altruists use: Where is your counterfactual impact greatest? For many of the ideas, there were people as good as me, if not better, to launch them. But if my co-founder, Aaron Boddy, and I had not launched a shrimp charity, it is very unlikely anyone would have done so at that moment. It was just too idiosyncratic. Once we looked into it, the argument was simple. Shrimp are the animals we raise and kill for food in the greatest numbers, by multiples: roughly half a trillion a year. And not a single person was working full-time on minimising the harms these likely sentient beings might face in the food system.

item.title: The First Way of Not Being There: Detachment
item.description:
Dissociation

The First Way of Not Being There: Detachment

Numbness, depersonalization, and derealization share one mechanism.

Posted November 14, 2026

Key points
  • Detachment lets us stay aware of what is happening while the brain lowers how strongly we feel it.
  • The prefrontal cortex can brake emotion too hard, muting feeling before it is felt.
  • Emotional numbing, physical numbness, depersonalization, and derealization share the same mechanism.
  • Detachment usually lifts on its own, but fear of it can make it last longer or keep coming back.

The term dissociation, as we use it today, carries so much in just one word that it has become hard to understand what people are referring to when they say they are dissociating. This confusion exists not only in pop culture but also in the professional field. The term's popularity has made it a common protagonist in the lives of many people who use it to describe all sorts of sensations that scare them to the point of alarm. The literature also uses the term to name several mechanisms and a large number of manifestations. So, I'm trying to help separate them, as I have always been very interested in precision. I believe that if we want to understand ourselves and find solutions to our emotional problems, it's better to know what we are treating.

And it's not only me. Many people in the field have become active in developing better explanations and new ways to identify differences among dissociative experiences.

My last post was the first in a new series on dissociation where I described four concrete and different mechanisms that cause dissociative experiences. This post explains one of the four in detail: Detachment.

To explain detachment, let me start with an example. Lisa got a call from the hospital informing her that her father had had a stroke. She rushed to the hospital and remained calm while talking to the doctors, signing forms, calling her brother, and arranging for someone to pick up her kids. She was a little surprised by how little emotion she felt, but three days later, standing in her kitchen, she started sobbing and couldn't stop. She called me because she wanted to work on what she experienced.

Detachment is one of the main mechanisms behind dissociative experiences, and it's the one that situations like Lisa's may recruit to help deal with them. In detachment, the person remains aware of what is happening and what it means. Lisa knew the gravity of her father's situation. What the mechanism did was to manage how strongly she felt her emotions. Research suggests that the prefrontal cortex, which normally helps regulate emotion, applies the brakes harder on the emotional system, turning down the volume of the experience. That’s why Lisa was able to be present to handle the situation without becoming overwhelmed.

Just think about it. If she had to deal with what she was feeling and also with all the other tasks the situation required, she probably wouldn't have been able to concentrate or make the decisions she had to make. That's why the brain “lowers the volume” of the emotions. Our own sedatives also help. Under this type of intense stress, the brain releases natural opioids that reduce pain and blunt feelings.

Detachment shows up in different ways, depending on what the brain is turning down.

Source: Adonyi Gábor / Pexels

Emotional numbing. What Lisa experienced belongs here. Feeling is turned down. The person knows that something matters but can't really feel it. When people detach this way, they often say, “I know I should feel something.”

Physical numbness. This type is similar, but it's more somatic. What gets turned down are bodily sensations and pain. Soldiers and accident victims sometimes don't notice serious injuries until hours later.

Depersonalization. This is one version of detachment that scares many people because, when the volume is turned down, they feel as if the experience doesn't belong to them. Signals from inside the body, which normally tell us “this is me, this is happening to me,” seem to carry less weight. Brain studies have linked depersonalization to reduced activity in the insula, a region that processes those inner signals. People may feel like observers of their own lives: Their hands look like someone else's, their voice sounds strange, or they watch themselves from a few feet away. The process is meant to be temporary, and it's not dangerous on its own. It feels weird, but if the person doesn’t fight it or keep checking whether it’s gone, it may subside relatively quickly. It can be problematic if it becomes chronic, and fear of the experience can contribute to its persistence. What I mean is that fearing it may be one reason it keeps happening, and if it keeps happening, it can become a regular response of the system when there is a threat.

Derealization. This version of detachment works in a similar way to depersonalization, but what is turned down is the felt sense of the outside world instead of the felt sense of the self. Everything looks right, but it doesn't feel familiar or real. A person may say their own street looks like a movie set, or that there is glass between them and everything else. What's missing is the sense of reality that usually comes with what we see. Like depersonalization, it can be temporary and is not dangerous on its own. It doesn't necessarily cause harm to the system or leave consequences once it's over. If the brain doesn't recover its baseline, the person may become more sensitive, feel overwhelmed more easily, and predict that the detachment will return. That can make the mechanism more likely to recur, causing fear and maintaining the cycle of increasing sensitivity.

To address the mechanism, in all four versions, there are a couple of steps to keep in mind:

  • After an accident or injury, get checked even if you feel no pain.
  • Tell yourself that it will pass and that your system is trying to protect you. That way, you may be less afraid of it, which can help reduce the activation contributing to the experience.
  • Gradually rebuild contact with your feelings, your body, and your sense of who you are.

If you notice yourself going numb or feeling unreal, it may help to ask what your system is turning down, and why now. If it’s helping, stay there and give it time to find the assurance that you don’t need it anymore.
